initial_requirements: The National Library of Medicine needs a digital repository for collection materials produced by existing and future digitization projects. Members of the public and NIH staff should be able to discover and view permitted materials, while authorized library staff need to create and maintain metadata, ingest or update digital objects, and manage their long-term preservation. Access may vary according to rights and user circumstances.

Staff should be able to review the original preserved bitstream, edit the placeholder or restricted metadata, update the rights decision when it changes, and trigger a release or make the item public once the object is cleared for access. Those actions should be tracked for auditability so it is clear who changed what and when. Keep version history for meaningful changes, especially anything affecting the content, rights, or preservation copy; routine metadata fixes should not create a new formal version every time, but the system should still audit those changes. Prior content versions should generally be retained as long as policy allows, subject to any retention rules confirmed with records and legal staff. If the preservation copy itself changes, create a new formal version; if only routine metadata changes, audit trail is enough unless the metadata change affects access, rights, or descriptive identity in a meaningful way, in which case include both a version note and an audit record; if both preservation-copy and routine metadata changes happen together, do both.

slots.key: Rights metadata used to determine access
slots.value: Access may vary according to rights; public and NIH access to approved content, with changing access rules over time, and access must be role-based and sometimes item-specific, with controls over what can be viewed, downloaded, or edited by each type of user. Rights and compliance should be the deciding factor when access, preservation, ingest speed, or collection-specific needs point in different directions. Staff should follow the standard process unless there is a documented, approved exception that applies to that specific collection or item. The exception should be tied to a named authority, be current, and be visible in the record so staff can justify why they did not use the default rule. If there’s any doubt, the default should win until a manager or rights authority confirms the exception. Anonymous users should be able to search and view only materials explicitly permitted for public access, and anything not cleared for public viewing should be blocked at the access control step. slots.key: Work preservation during outages
Recovery and resumption behavior
slots.value: In-progress staff work should ideally resume automatically if the system can safely pick up where it left off, especially for batch ingest, metadata edits, or queued preservation actions. If an operation was interrupted in a way that leaves uncertainty, staff should have to restart or confirm it rather than the system guessing. User requests should stay queued or receive a clear failure message so they can retry once service is back. If a request is safe to retry without duplicating anything or changing the outcome, it should stay queued for automatic completion; if there’s any risk of duplicate ingest, duplicate notification, or an access decision being applied twice, it should be marked failed and left for manual retry. Rights-related changes and preservation writes should be handled more cautiously than simple viewing or download requests. Public anonymous requests can usually be retried automatically if they’re simple read-only actions like viewing a permitted item. Staff actions, especially anything that changes metadata, rights, or preservation content, should be treated more cautiously and usually need manual confirmation if they were interrupted.

slots.key: Post-maintenance validation expectations
Security controls for public and staff access
slots.value: Role-based access with item-specific controls; users are blocked cleanly when their role or item-level permission does not allow viewing, downloading, or editing an object or its metadata. The system should explain denial in plain language without exposing hidden details, and where possible guide users to the next step, such as requesting access or contacting the appropriate staff group. Public users should get a simple, non-technical message that the item isn’t available to view or download due to rights or access restrictions, and if there is a legitimate path to request access, the message should point to it; otherwise it can just explain that the content is restricted. Library staff should get a more specific message that directs them to the correct internal contact or workflow when their role doesn’t allow the action, without revealing anything sensitive about the item itself. Public users may see only basic descriptive information but not the file itself; staff may be able to view a record but not edit or publish it. If rights status is unclear, public access should be restricted until authorized staff verify the status; if rights are mixed, the most restrictive applicable rule governs public visibility, while staff may retain broader internal access if allowed. Readiness checks should confirm that authorized staff can create and edit metadata, ingest or update objects, and assign rights or access settings without needing manual data fixes outside the system. They should also verify consistent enforcement for public users, NIH staff, and repository staff, including restricted, mixed, or unpublished materials, and prove that the same item appears differently depending on user role and rights status, with results staying correct after updates. Public search and viewing should stay available during spikes as long as the system can safely support it; if throttling is needed for stability, it should protect the system first and favor authenticated staff for administrative functions while keeping public discovery and viewing available as much as possible. When preservation and access rules conflict, preserve the content safely but do not expose it publicly until the rights decision is final; preferably show only a minimal restricted representation such as a metadata record or placeholder if staff want the item discoverable without revealing the content, and if even that is too risky, hide it from general users and make it visible only to authorized staff until resolved. Staff should be able to review the original preserved bitstream, edit the placeholder or restricted metadata, update the rights decision when it changes, trigger a release or make the item public once the review is complete and the object is cleared for access, and have those actions tracked for auditability so it is clear who changed what and when. Download and reuse should follow the rights status of the item, so if something is open it can be downloaded, but if rights are restricted the system should limit copying or hide the download option. Role matters too, because NIH staff may need broader access than the general public for some internal or restricted collections. Collection-specific conditions can override the general rule when there are donor restrictions, privacy concerns, or other special handling requirements.

slots.key: Highest-priority repository capabilities
slots.value: Rights compliance and preservation integrity first; accurate ingest and metadata second; discovery convenience third. Main outcomes are making permitted materials easy to discover and view, getting new digitized content into the repository accurately, and preserving digital objects over the long term, with staff able to maintain metadata and manage rights correctly. More advanced discovery features, such as richer search facets and recommendation-style browsing, can wait if core ingest, rights, and preservation tasks remain reliable.
